about_page.para1: Global Pollution Watch (GPW) is an open-source pollution mapping and risk assessment tool which can support managers, scientists, and citizen scientists to identify and address land-based pollution risks impacting tropical coastal environments.
about_page.para2: In over 100 countries with watersheds draining into tropical waters, the tool quantifies and maps pollution loads generated on land as well as pollution exposure in downstream coastal environments across 20 years (2000-2020). Pollution loads and exposures are based on the results of spatially explicit models developed from globally available datasets.
about_page.para3: Under the beta version of Global Pollution Watch, users can explore the generation and impact of sediment pollution from land use change and deforestation. Sediment pollution data is available for watersheds > 500 hectares that drain into tropical waters, and is modelled using linked land-sea models. On land, sediment load is modelled using the sediment delivery ratio model within the Natural Capital Project's <invest>InVEST®</invest> toolkit, and in the sea, sediment exposure in coastal waters is modelled using a newly developed marine pollution transport model, CoaSTED. See Science & Methods for further details.
about_page.para4: Global Pollution Watch is developed by the Wildlife Conservation Society, Fluvio, Sparkgeo – Applied Geospatial, and The University of Queensland; powered by MERMAID; and funded by G20 CORDAP (Coral Research & Development Accelerator Platform).
about_page.contact_para: We would love your feedback, please contact us at <email>info@globalpollutionwatch.org</email>.

note_to_users.para1: The models underpinning GPW are currently undergoing calibration and refinement. The release of the Beta version is intended to capture feedback on tool features and functionality, but the currently displayed results may change as the model outputs are refined.

land_use.para1: Land cover and land use maps were developed for the years 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2020 from the GLAD global land cover and land use change dataset [1]. The original GLAD dataset contains 109 land use subclasses which were reclassified into six classes for visualisation:
land_use.missing_coverage_intro: Several countries and territories with watersheds draining into tropical waters are either not covered or only partially covered by the GLAD dataset and therefore are missing land use data within the tool. These are:
missing_coverage_countries: St Helena Ascension and Tristan da Cunha

sediment_load.para1: Sediment load is the amount of overland (hillslope) soil erosion that is delivered from land to streams. It does not capture streambank or gully erosion and in places where this form of erosion is more prevalent, the sediment load data displayed here may be a significant underestimation [2,3]. Pixel values represent the metric tons of sediment per hectare that is delivered to streams from each land pixel. Watershed values represent the total tons of sediment delivered to streams from across the whole watershed.
sediment_load.para2: We calculated these sediment load values using the widely used sediment delivery ratio model within the Natural Capital Project's InVEST® toolkit (version 3.15.1 [4]). We ran InVEST for every year with land use data available (see Land use), limiting our analysis to watersheds that are 500 hectares or bigger due to the heavy computational requirements by running the model at a global scale.
sediment_load.para3: In summary, the sediment delivery ratio model estimates annual sediment loads by modelling potential soil loss over land and hydrological connectivity between sources of sediment and downstream "sinks" (i.e., streams that receive sediment). The model runs at the resolution of an input digital elevation model, which is 90 m resolution for Global Pollution Watch, and requires additional spatial inputs of rainfall erosivity, soil erodibility, slope, and land cover.
sediment_load.para4: See Hamel et al. [5] for full model description and tables below for inputs used to parameterise the model for watersheds greater than 500 hectares draining into tropical coastal waters.
sediment_load.table1_caption: Table 1 – Parameterisation of InVEST sediment delivery ratio model

table1_rows.parameterisation: MERIT Hydro: hydrologically conditioned global digital elevation model [6]
Global rainfall erosivity developed by Panagos et al. [8] interpolated to match the extent of the watershed polygon
Global soil erodibility developed by Gupta et al. [9] interpolated to match the extent of the watershed polygon
GLAD global land cover and land use change dataset [1] reclassified into 14 classes based on erosion characteristics (see Table 2)
This defines the cover management factor and protection factor for each land use/cover category. See Table 2 for full values.

sediment_load.table1_note: Note: All spatial data inputs were reprojected to Mollweide (EPSG:54009) to meet model requirements of a metric-based projection
sediment_load.table2_caption: Table 2 – Biophysical table input for InVEST sediment delivery ratio model

sediment_exposure.para1: 'Sediment exposure' is the time-integrated weight of land-based sediment pollution reaching coastal waters, summarised in metric tons per hectare. It represents the annual average dispersal and movement of sediment and the exposure of ecosystems. We estimate this using a newly developed marine pollution transport model, CoaSTED, which models the transport of sediment loads from each watershed (see Sediment Load) into the adjacent coastal waters. After the marine transport of sediment loads is calculated from each watershed, the total pollution exposure is calculated by summing the marine sediment loads from all watersheds.
sediment_exposure.para2: CoaSTED considers the influence of river discharge velocity and flow direction, tidal currents, ocean currents, and bathymetry to capture the likely movement and deposition of land-based sediment loads as they travel from river mouths through coastal waters. This represents a large improvement in marine pollution transport modelling from the commonly used distance-decay models which fail to capture complex sediment transport dynamics. CoaSTED was used to calculate sediment exposure from watersheds greater than 500 hectares draining into tropical coastal waters, so does not currently capture sediment dispersal from smaller watersheds, which may also be impacting coastal ecosystems.
sediment_exposure.para3: CoaSTED is currently undergoing model calibration but it will differ from how satellites capture sediment exposure, as it disperses sediment through settlement and resuspension using conditions found throughout the year.

benthic_layers.para1: Global coral reef benthic habitats are from the Allen Coral Atlas [22], which define seven classes of habitat:

classes.description: The location of shallow coral reef features generally seen from satellites
Any hardbottom area supporting living coral and/or algae
Any habitat where seagrass is the dominant biota
Visible accumulations of microscopic algae in sandy sediments
Any exposed hardbottom area with uncommon to scarce corals and fleshy macroalgae
Any habitat featuring loose, rough fragments of broken reef material
Any soft-bottom area dominated by fine unconsolidated sediments

benthic_layers.outro: See the Allen Coral Atlas [22] for further information.

ecosystem_extent.para1: 'Ecosystem extent exposed to pollution' is the area/extent of coral/algae, seagrass, and reef ecosystems exposed to pollution, summarised in hectares. We calculate this by overlaying the corresponding benthic habitats (see Benthic layers) with the extent of ocean exposed to sediment pollution (see Sediment exposure) to isolate the area of each ecosystem exposed to pollution.

contributing_watersheds.para1: The top three 'contributing watersheds' represented in the tool are the three watersheds contributing the most sediment to the selected ocean pixel. We also provide the percentage contribution from each of these watersheds to the total sediment exposure at the pixel. We estimate this using a newly developed marine pollution transport model, CoaSTED, which models the transport of sediment loads from each watershed into the adjacent coastal waters. See Sediment exposure for further details.
